prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

There once was a Square, such a square little Square, And he loved a trim Triangle; But she was a flirt and around her skirt Vainly she made him dangle. Oh he wanted to wed and he had no dread Of domestic woes and wrangles; For he thought that his fate was to procreate Cute little Squares and Triangles. Now it happened one day on that geometric way There swaggered a big bold Cube, With a haughty stare and he made that Square Have the air of a perfect boob; To his solid spell the Triangle fell, And she thrilled with love’s sweet sickness, For she took delight in his breadth and height— But how she adored his thickness! So that poor little Square just died of despair, For his love he could not strangle; While the bold Cube led to the bridal bed That cute and acute Triangle. The Square’s sad lot she has long forgot, And his passionate pretensions ... For she dotes on her kids—Oh such cute Pyramids In a world of three dimensions.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: There, Square, And

outputs.L1:
There once was a Square, such a square little Square,  
And he loved a trim Triangle;  
But she was a flirt, and around her skirt  
Vainly she made him dangle.

Oh, he wanted to wed, and he had no dread  
Of domestic woes and wrangles,  
For he thought that his fate was to procreate  
Cute little Squares and Triangles.

Now, it happened one day, on that geometric way,  
There swaggered a big, bold Cube.  
With a haughty stare, he made that Square  
Have the air of a perfect boob.

To his solid spell the Triangle fell,  
And she thrilled with love’s sweet sickness,  
For she took delight in his breadth and height—  
But, oh, how she adored his thickness!

So that poor little Square just died of despair,  
For his love he could not strangle,  
While the bold Cube led to the bridal bed  
That cute and acute Triangle.

The Square’s sad lot she has long forgot,  
And his passionate pretensions,  
For she dotes on her kids—oh, such cute Pyramids!—  
In a world of three dimensions.
outputs.L2:
Once lived a neat little Square who fell deeply in love with a graceful Triangle. Yet she was coquettish, keeping him hopefully waiting while she played with his affection. He dreamed of marrying her and felt no fear of household troubles or marital disputes, imagining that together they would raise charming little Squares and Triangles.

Then, one day along their geometric path, a large, self-assured Cube came striding by. His proud manner made the Square seem utterly foolish and insignificant. The Triangle was immediately captivated by the Cube’s three-dimensional charm and became giddy with love. She admired his width and height, but it was his depth that enchanted her most.

Unable to overcome his love, the unfortunate Square wasted away from heartbreak. Meanwhile, the daring Cube married the lovely, sharp-angled Triangle. She soon forgot the Square’s miserable fate and earnest romantic hopes, devoting herself instead to their delightful children: adorable Pyramids living in a three-dimensional world.
outputs.L3:
A little Square falls deeply in love with a beautiful but flirtatious Triangle. Captivated by her sharp elegance, he dreams of marrying her and building a peaceful life together. In his imagination, their home is filled with happy children—little Squares and Triangles who combine the finest qualities of both parents.

Their romance is disrupted, however, by the arrival of a bold and impressive Cube. Unlike the flat Square, the Cube possesses not only length and width but also height and thickness. His commanding three-dimensional presence makes the Square appear plain and inadequate by comparison.

The Triangle is immediately drawn to the Cube’s greater depth and stature. Forgetting the devotion of her former admirer, she abandons the Square, who is left heartbroken and ultimately dies of despair. The Triangle soon marries the Cube and enters his richer, three-dimensional world. There, she forgets the unfortunate Square entirely and delights in raising their Pyramid children, content with the grand new life she has chosen.
outputs.L4:
Square had always loved Triangle. He admired her graceful angles, her sharp wit, and the way she could balance perfectly on a single point. Together they roamed their flat, two-dimensional world, tracing patterns across the page and imagining a future side by side.

Then Cube arrived.

He resembled Square, but there was something undeniably more impressive about him. He had depth. He could turn, tumble, and reveal one face after another, while Square remained forever flat. Triangle was fascinated by this mysterious newcomer and the dimension he brought into her life. Though Square tried to win her back with perfect symmetry and four dependable sides, he could not compete with Cube’s solid charm.

Triangle and Cube soon fell in love. Their union crossed the boundary between the flat and the solid, combining her triangular elegance with his three-dimensional substance. In time, they produced a lively family of Pyramids—figures with triangular faces, solid bodies, and points reaching proudly upward.

Square was heartbroken, but even he had to admit that the children were remarkable. And so the curious romance became a playful lesson in geometry: when a two-dimensional Triangle meets the depth of a three-dimensional form, entirely new shapes—and new life—can emerge.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a humorous narrative poem about a Square who loves a Triangle, only to lose her to a three-dimensional Cube.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Square, the Triangle, and the Cube**

There once was a Square in a flat little town,  
With four equal sides and a permanent frown.  
He loved a young Triangle, graceful and bright,  
With three lovely angles—all perfectly acute.

He’d wait by her corner each morning at eight,  
And whisper, “Dear Triangle, please be my mate.  
Our shapes may be different, but surely you’ll see—  
You’re the hypotenuse missing from me.”

She blushed at this compliment, though it was wrong  
(She wasn’t right-angled, but played along).  
They picnicked on graph paper, danced on a plane,  
And measured their courtship with ruler and chain.

Then into their village, one terrible day,  
A stranger appeared in a three-dimensional way.  
He swaggered through town with considerable flair:  
Six faces, twelve edges—the bold Mister Cube.

The Square took one look and cried, “What a brute!  
He’s merely six squares in a box-shaped suit!”  
But Triangle stared, and her angles went weak.  
“He has so much depth,” she said with a squeak.

The Cube gave a bow. “Come away, if you please.  
I own a fine mansion on X, Y, and Z.  
Why stay on this plane, where existence is flat?  
I’ve volume, dear lady. What do you think of that?”

Poor Square puffed himself to seem broader and tall,  
But being two-dimensional didn’t help at all.  
He challenged the Cube: “I demand that we fight!”  
The Cube merely rolled—and crushed him outright.

Now Triangle lives in a spacious glass prism,  
Discussing perspective and postmodernism.  
While Square haunts the graph paper, bitter and blue,  
Still muttering, “Honestly—what’s she see in that Cube?”

Yet time healed his heart, as time often can,  
And Square met a Circle who quite liked his span.  
They opened a diner called **Corners & Pies**,  
Where shapes come for comfort—and Cube pays full price.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a playful, rhyming geometric love triangle featuring personified shapes and ending with the birth of pyramids.
counterfactuals.output:
Miss Circle swooned for Triangle’s flair,  
While Triangle blushed for dashing Square.  
But Square, with four neat sides to spare,  
Loved rolling Circle everywhere.

They sighed, “Our hearts won’t form a line—  
This tangled shape is by design!”  
So Circle drew a wedding ring,  
And angles danced a quadrille swing.

Square made a base, triangles climbed,  
Their edges kissed, their corners rhymed.  
Then—pop!—beneath the desert skids,  
Their love gave birth to pyramids!
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a witty ballad in which a lovesick two-dimensional Square is rejected when an alluring Triangle falls for a bold Cube because of his “thickness.”
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Ballad of Square’s Thin Affair**

A lovesick Square in Planeville dwelt,  
With corners trim and true;  
But flat was every hope he felt  
When Triangle came in view.  

She had three angles, sharp and sly,  
A point that turned each head;  
“Dear Triangle, be mine,” sighed he—  
“You’re acute,” was all he said.  

She smiled along her longest side:  
“You’re equal, neat, and fair,  
But every time I look at you,  
There’s simply nothing *there*.”  

Then through the plane strode gallant Cube,  
A bold, substantial beau;  
He cast a shadow broad and deep  
And boomed a bass “Hello.”  

Six faces flashed, twelve edges gleamed;  
He flexed his vertices.  
Poor Square could only stand and stare—  
Or lie there, if you please.  

Fair Triangle took Cube’s thick arm:  
“At last—a solid match!  
He’s got the depth I’ve dreamed about,  
And quite a three-D catch.”  

Square cried, “But I have perfect sides!  
My angles all are right!”  
She sighed, “You’re lovely on the page,  
But he can hold me tight.”  

So Cube and Triangle rolled off,  
While Square stayed on the sheet;  
He learned that love, like geometry,  
Can add dimensions to defeat.  

Yet Square now dates a Rhombus, who  
Admires his planar chic:  
“She says I’m deep in character—  
Though technically not thick.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a whimsical poem about romance across dimensions, using mathematical puns, an acute Triangle, a jealous Square, and a swaggering Cube.
counterfactuals.output:
In Flatland’s glow, where moonbeams lie,  
An acute Triangle caught an eye.  
Her angles sweet, her wit so right,  
She made the parallel stars unite.

A Square, quite jealous, stiff and prim,  
Declared, “Her love should corner him!  
I’m fair and equal, side for side—  
A perfect match!” he squared with pride.

Then through the plane, with cosmic boom,  
A swaggering Cube strode into the room.  
“Make space,” he grinned, “I’ve depth to spare—  
Your romance, friends, is rather square.”

The Triangle blushed a rosy sine.  
“Dear Cube, your volume is divine,  
But love’s no theorem to construe—  
It multiplies in dimensions two.”

The Square cried, “Wait! That can’t be true!  
My heart has four right angles too!”  
She said, “Don’t be obtuse, dear Square—  
There’s more than one solution there.”

So hand in edge, through space they flew,  
Past axis red and vector blue.  
Their paths converged, their fears grew small—  
For love, they learned, transcends them all.

And somewhere past infinity,  
They danced in strange geometry:  
A point, a plane, a heart’s sweet arc—  
Three shapes aligned among the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you produce a comic verse about anthropomorphic geometric figures, with regular rhymes, risqué double entendres, and a punchline involving cute little pyramids in a three-dimensional world?
counterfactuals.output:
Miss Circle wore a daring arc and winked across the square,  
While Rhombus flashed his angles like a rogue without a care.  
Sir Cylinder bragged loudly of his length and polished base,  
And Sphere confessed, “I like a form that rolls with style and grace.”  

Miss Cone said, “Mind my pointed wit—it often gets me dates,”  
Then Cube replied, “I’m solid, dear, and good on all six faces.”  
They slipped behind a tangent where the lines were getting blurred,  
And proved that “strictly parallel” is often just a word.  

But when their little offspring bounced in, everyone could see:  
Cute baby pyramids—because **it takes three sides to raise a family in 3-D!**
